question: Why did Britain care so much about a frontier in the Middle East in the 1920s?
answer: Britain's concern stemmed from its mandate over Iraq and the belief that the Mosul vilayet was economically and strategically essential to Iraq's viability, including its potential oil resources and agricultural wealth, as well as Britain's broader imperial interests in the region as a link to India and the East.

evidence.passage: You cannot develop Iraq into anything that will maintain itself and help the Empire with markets—because I look at both aspects—unless it includes the Mosul area. Its revenues will not be sufficient. Its economic production will not be of an order to make itself sufficiently maintain its population.

That was the question of the future of Mosul, a point to which the Turks attached enormous importance, but the importance of which to us could not be for a moment denied, because of its necessity to the mandated territory of Mesopotamia, or, as it is now called, Iraq, which we were responsible for having set up.

question: Why couldn't Turkey and Britain just agree on the border themselves?
answer: Direct negotiations between Britain and Turkey over the Mosul frontier repeatedly failed to reach agreement, so the matter was referred to the League of Nations for a binding decision, with both parties agreeing to accept the League Council's ruling.

evidence.passage: The question of the Turco-Iraq frontier was referred to the Council of the League of Nations in accordance with Article 3 (2) of the Treaty of Lausanne. As a result, it has beers agreed at Geneva that the Council will delimit the frontier between Turkey and Iraq, and both the Turkish and British delegates have given undertakings that their respective Governments will accept any decision which the Council may adopt and will meanwhile maintain and respect the status quo, that is to say, the position as it stood at the time of the conclusion of the Treaty of Lausanne.

As regards Mosul, instead of fighting it out there—although we did discuss it at the table—instead of trying to find a solution there, we agreed to remit the matter to negotiations between the two Powers, and these negotiations are about to begin at Constantinople. If they are unsuccessful, then we provide in the Treaty for the reference of the matter to the League of Nations.

question: Was oil the real reason behind the Mosul dispute?
answer: This was hotly disputed in Parliament. Critics like Thurtle, Wallhead, and Kenworthy argued oil was the real motive behind British policy, while Sir Austen Chamberlain strongly denied this, pointing out that Britain had rejected a Turkish offer in March 1925 that would have given Britain all the oil concessions in exchange for ceding most of Mosul to Turkey.

evidence.passage: If we were after oil, we could have had a concession for all the oil in Mosul and concessions for anything else we liked. The reply of His Majesty's Government was that they were trustees for Iraq; that they were not possessors, but mandatories, and that as mandatories and trustees they could not bargain away the rights and interests of Iraq and her people in exchange for concessions to British capitalists. There never was a shameful allegation made with less shadow of foundation.
It is said that Mosul has nothing whatever to do with oil. I want to ask one question. Assume for a moment that Mosul was a cabbage patch. Would you be there? You would not be there at all.

question: What did the people living in the disputed area actually want?
answer: Accounts conflicted: some MPs who visited reported the local population strongly welcomed British rule and the League's decision, fearing a return of Turkish rule, while others argued the population was split, with many families divided between pro-Turk and pro-British sentiment due to fear of Turkish vengeance.

evidence.passage: I had the privilege of talking to a very great many, not only of the big men in the country, but to the small men, and all over, and on every side I found an intense desire for the British occupation and the British lead to establish Iraq on a, firm basis extended from one side of the country to the other side.

When we got there, we found that 50 per cent. of the members of the large families were pro-Turk and the other 56 per cent. were pro-British. The reason for that was simply fear of the return of the Turk—fear of the vengeance of the Turk if by any chance he returned.

question: Did Britain accept the League's decision?

history.content: What was the Mosul dispute about?

answer: Yes. The British representative at the League Council gave a definite undertaking that the British Government would abide by the Council's decision regarding the Mosul frontier, and this was confirmed as still binding in 1925.

evidence.passage: whether the British representative at the thirteenth session of the League of Nations Council gave a definite undertaking that the British Government would abide by the Council's decision; if so, whether His Majesty's Government considers itself still bound by that pledge; and whether a similar undertaking was given by the Turkish representative?
The answers to the three remaining parts of the question are in the affirmative.

question: What did the government decide about the treaty?

history.content: Tell me about the Mosul question after Lausanne.

answer: Both the Turkish National Assembly and the Iraq Parliament authorised ratification of the Mosul boundary treaty, and the British government decided to proceed with ratification at the earliest possible moment, with His Majesty to be advised to ratify within a few days unless a parliamentary discussion was requested.

evidence.passage: Both the Turkish National Assembly and the Iraq Parliament have authorised the ratification of the Treaty forthwith; it is eminently desirable that the British ratification should be given at the earliest possible moment. Unless, therefore, the right hon. Gentleman desires a discussion on the Treaty in this House, His Majesty will be advised to ratify in a few days.

question: How did the League end up deciding who got the islands between Finland and Sweden?
answer: Not stated in these documents; they cover referral of the dispute, the advisory opinion of jurists, and the appointment of a Commission of Rapporteurs to study and recommend a settlement, but no final decision on sovereignty is given here.

question: Why did the islanders want to join Sweden instead of staying with Finland?
answer: The documents do not explain the islanders' motivations for wanting to join Sweden.

question: What did the Commission recommend?

history.content: How did the Aaland Islands question reach the League?

answer: The documents do not include the Commission's recommendations; they only note that the Commission of Rapporteurs was appointed and that its report was later published separately by the League of Nations in 1921.

question: Did Finland accept the outcome?

history.content: Why did the Aaland islanders want to join Sweden?

answer: The documents do not state whether Finland accepted the outcome.

question: Why did the League fail to get Poland out of Vilna?
answer: The League of Nations was not able to force Poland out of Vilna; instead, responsibility for deciding Vilna's fate was ultimately handed to the Ambassadors' Conference, which decided in Poland's favor using authority from the Treaty of Versailles rather than any League mandate. The League had asked the parties to accept proposed conditions, but Poland and Lithuania rejected those terms, so the matter reverted to the Allied Powers who awarded Vilna to Poland.

evidence.passage: No, Sir; it is not correct to say that it was handed over to the League of Nations. The League of Nations were informally asked if they would devise conditions and submit them to the parties interested. They did so, and the parties, as a matter of fact, rejected those terms; consequently, the responsibility for a decision was thrown back upon the Allied and Associated Powers.

The answer to the first part of the question is in the affirmative. The Ambassadors' Conference derives the authority to take such a decision from Article 87 of the Treaty of Versailles, which stipulates that the boundaries of Poland not laid down in the Treaty will be subsequently determined by the Principal Allied and Associated Powers.

question: Why did the League fail there?
answer: The League's Vilna Commission could not even secure an armistice, as Polish irregular forces under General Zeligowski (disowned by the Polish government) kept attacking the Lithuanians despite the League's involvement, and when the League later tried to mediate a settlement by proposing conditions, both Poland and Lithuania rejected the terms, so the League's role effectively ended and the dispute was resolved instead by the Ambassadors' Conference awarding Vilna to Poland under Treaty of Versailles authority.

evidence.passage: According to our latest information, General Seligowski, who has been publicly disowned by the Polish Government, is continuing his attacks against the Lithuanians, the League of Nations Commission having not yet succeeded in arranging an armistice.

No, Sir; it is not correct to say that it was handed over to the League of Nations. The League of Nations were informally asked if they would devise conditions and submit them to the parties interested. They did so, and the parties, as a matter of fact, rejected those terms; consequently, the responsibility for a decision was thrown back upon the Allied and Associated Powers.

question: Which disputes did the League of Nations manage to settle in the early 1920s?
answer: The League of Nations handled the Aaland Islands dispute between Sweden and Finland, successfully referring it to a commission and Council for settlement; it also handled the Mosul/Iraq-Turkey frontier dispute, with a Commission investigating and the Council ultimately delimiting the frontier; and it was involved in the Polish-Lithuanian dispute over Vilna, though with less success in fully resolving it.

evidence.passage: As stated by hon. Friend the Under-Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs on the 23rd June, in reply to a question by my hon. Friend the Member for Lincoln, the Secretary of State, acting in exercise of the friendly right conferred by Article XI. of the Covenant of the League of Nations, has brought to the attention of the Council of the League the case of the Aaland Islands as a matter affecting international relations, which unfortunately threatens to disturb the good understanding between nations upon whom peace depends. He has informed the Governments of Sweden and Finland of the action which he felt it his duty to take, and both Governments have expressed their satisfaction that the case will now be examined without delay.

The question of the Turco-Iraq frontier was referred to the Council of the League of Nations in accordance with Article 3 (2) of the Treaty of Lausanne. As a result, it has beers agreed at Geneva that the Council will delimit the frontier between Turkey and Iraq, and both the Turkish and British delegates have given undertakings that their respective Governments will accept any decision which the Council may adopt and will meanwhile maintain and respect the status quo, that is to say, the position as it stood at the time of the conclusion of the Treaty of Lausanne.

There is no tribunal in Brussels, as suggested. Monsieur Hymans has been delegated by the League of Nations to preside over conferences between Polish and Lithuanian delegates in Brussels, and will submit any solution that may be reached to the Council of the League of Nations for its decision.

question: In which of these disputes did a great power's own interests get in the way of the League?
answer: In the Upper Silesia dispute, British, French and Italian interests and disagreements among the Allied Powers themselves (rather than League mediation) shaped the outcome, with French military control of Allied troops causing friction, as Colonel Wedgwood pointed out when questioning whether the French command (sympathetic to Polish insurgents) prevented impartial resolution.

evidence.passage: Is not the whole military direction of the allied troops in Upper Silesia in the hands of the French, and can we expect any improvement as long as that military direction is in the hands of sympathisers with the Polish insurgents?

asked the Prime Minister whether any arrangements have yet been made for a conference to decide the fate of Upper Silesia; and whether British troops there are being employed in driving back German insurgents while French troops are carrying on their previous role in the area under the control of Polish insurgents?

question: How did Parliament react when the League's decisions went against British wishes?
answer: When the League's Commission report on Mosul leaned toward findings unfavorable to Iraq remaining under British influence, Ramsay MacDonald defended the government's position of accepting the League's decision regardless, while Amery disputed the characterization of the Commission's report, showing Parliamentary debate over how to react to League findings that cut against British interests.

evidence.passage: The right hon. Gentleman knows quite well that the Report of the Commission, which was the material for consideration at Geneva was one of those extraordinary Reports which, if the weight of it had been taken altogether, would have been in favour of Mosul going away from Iraq, historical evidence etc.
That is not the view which the League of Nations took of it.

question: Which disputes involved Poland, and how did they turn out?
answer: Poland was involved in the Upper Silesia plebiscite dispute with Germany, which was eventually handled through negotiations and an economic convention with a League-appointed chairman presiding over the mixed commission; and in the Polish-Lithuanian dispute over Vilna, which Poland effectively resolved in its favor through the Ambassadors' Conference awarding Vilna to Poland under Article 87 of the Treaty of Versailles, bypassing a full League of Nations decision after Lithuania and Poland rejected League-devised terms.

evidence.passage: The answer to the first part of the question is in the affirmative. The Ambassadors' Conference derives the authority to take such a decision from Article 87 of the Treaty of Versailles, which stipulates that the boundaries of Poland not laid down in the Treaty will be subsequently determined by the Principal Allied and Associated Powers.

No, Sir; it is not correct to say that it was handed over to the League of Nations. The League of Nations were informally asked if they would devise conditions and submit them to the parties interested. They did so, and the parties, as a matter of fact, rejected those terms; consequently, the responsibility for a decision was thrown back upon the Allied and Associated Powers.

Under the Treaty of Versailles (Section 6 of the Annex to Article 88) the powers of the Plebiscite Commission in Upper Silesia terminate when the parts of the area allotted to Germany and Poland have been placed under German and Polish administration. This cannot be done until the economic convention for the administration of the industrial area, now being negotiated between Germany and Poland under a chairman appointed by the League of Nations, has been concluded.

question: Why was the vote in Upper Silesia so controversial?
answer: Not clearly answerable from these documents. There is no passage explaining the specific controversy over the plebiscite vote itself (e.g., disputes over its fairness or methodology); the documents mostly concern troop deployments, casualties, and administrative questions rather than the reasons the vote was controversial.

question: Why were British troops sent to Silesia at all?
answer: British troops were sent to Upper Silesia to help the other Allied troops keep order in the plebiscite area.

evidence.passage: The force is intended to help the other Allied troops to keep order in the plebiscite area, and it will be drawn partly from the British Army on the Rhine, and partly from troops in the United Kingdom.

question: Who got the territory in the end?

history.content: What happened in the Upper Silesia plebiscite?

answer: The former plebiscite area was ultimately divided and transferred to the administration of the German and Polish Governments.

evidence.passage: The whole of the former plebiscite area has now, I believe, been transferred to the administration of the German and Polish Governments.

question: What was the cost of that, and who paid?

history.content: Why were Allied troops stationed in Upper Silesia?

answer: The cost of the British Army of Occupation on the Rhine and in Silesia for the period 1 April to 30 June 1922 was estimated at £600,000, and under the Treaty of Versailles this cost was chargeable to Poland and Germany, though Germany was not actually paying the bill.

evidence.passage: The cost of the British Army of Occupation on the Rhine and in Silesia for the period 1st April to 30th June, 1922, is estimated at £600,000.
The cost is chargeable to Poland and Germany under the terms of the Treaty of Versailles.
What is the use of charging this to Germany when she is not paying the bill?

question: How quickly did the League act when fighting broke out on the Greek-Bulgarian border, and why did it work?
answer: The League acted quickly in the Greco-Bulgarian dispute: fighting was stopped first, with each country required to withdraw its troops from the other's territory, and only after that did arbitration follow. Lord Cecil cites this as the normal, healthy way arbitration is established—security first, then arbitration.

evidence.passage: it is worth observing that in the Græco-Bulgarian dispute, which has just taken place, you first stop the fighting, you first require each country to withdraw its troops from the other country, and then arbitration follows as a matter of course. I believe that to be, I will not say the only way in which arbitration will be established, but the normal, usual and healthy way in which it will be established.

question: Did Britain take part?

history.content: What did Parliament discuss about the League loans to Greece and Bulgaria?

answer: Britain had not committed to participating; Sir Austen Chamberlain repeatedly said he could not say in advance what the British Government's attitude would be to such a League-organised loan for Bulgaria, while noting the similar Greek loan scheme had been working, albeit with difficulty.

evidence.passage: I cannot undertake to say in advance what would be the attitude of His Majesty's Government in the event of the League's under taking to organise such a loan.

It is now working well, but it has not worked without difficulty, and, though I recognise the importance, for peace in these districts, of the settlement of these refugees, I should be unwilling to make any statement in general terms about a loan brought out under the auspices of the League.
